turns.prompt_text: My compass sat next to a pair of scissors which happened to be mildly magnetic over the course of a few days. The compass eventually was offset by this. Do magnetic forces saddle and become more potent or stronger?
turns.response_html:
What you are experiencing with your compass isn't actually the magnetic force growing stronger or "saddling" over time. Instead, you are seeing the results of magnetic induction and a phenomenon called remanence.

Here is exactly what happened between your scissors and your compass, and how magnetic materials behave under pressure.

1. Do Magnetic Forces "Build Up"?

No, magnetic fields do not compound, stack, or become stronger on their own just by sitting next to each other. The actual force exerted by the scissors didn't increase.

However, exposure over time matters because of how magnetic domains move inside a material.

2. Why Your Compass Changed (Magnetic Remanence)

Inside the steel needle of your compass are microscopic regions called magnetic domains. Think of them as billions of tiny, microscopic bar magnets.

  • Before exposure: In a properly functioning compass, these domains are permanently aligned so that the needle points toward Earth's magnetic north.
  • During exposure: The scissors, though only "mildly magnetic," had a strong enough local field to challenge Earth's relatively weak magnetic field. Over a few days, that constant, close-proximity magnetic pressure forced the microscopic domains inside the compass needle to slowly physically rotate and realign themselves with the scissors' field instead of Earth's.
  • The Result: Your compass needle was partially demagnetized and then remagnetized in a new, flawed direction. The needle now has a permanent "offset" because its internal domains are stuck in that new alignment. This remaining magnetization is called remanence.

3. The "Saddle" Concept (Magnetic Hysteresis)

While forces don't compound, magnetic materials do have a sort of memory, which is perfectly described by a hysteresis loop.

If you expose a magnetic material to an external field, it resists changing at first. But as the field is applied continuously (or grows stronger), the material reaches a tipping point where its domains flip. Once they flip, they don't just snap back when the source is removed; they stay "saddled" in that new state until an equally strong opposite force pushes them back.

How to Fix Your Compass

Because the compass needle is made of a hard magnetic material (usually steel), you can actually fix it using a strong magnet (like a neodymium refrigerator magnet or a magnetic tool organizer).

  1. Identify North: Use a phone GPS or a known good compass to figure out true magnetic North.
  2. Realign the Domains: Take the north pole of your strong magnet and scrape it along the compass needle, starting from the center pivot and pulling outward toward the tip you want to be North.
  3. Lift and Repeat: Lift the magnet far away, bring it back to the center, and stroke outward again. Repeating this 10 to 15 times will force those microscopic domains to snap back into their proper alignment.

Keep that compass away from your toolbox, speakers, and magnetic scissors in the future! Did you want to try re-magnetizing it, or are you just curious about the physics behind it?
